title: Setting Aside an Ex Parte Decree

scenes.dialogue: A money decree, in a suit you never knew about. Now your bank account is attached. Can that decree be undone?
Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. Today, Order Nine, Rule Thirteen of the C P C: setting aside an ex parte decree.
scenes.shown: Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. Today, Order IX Rule 13 of the CPC: setting aside an ex parte decree.

scenes.dialogue: An ex parte decree is passed in the defendant's absence, after the suit is heard without him.
Order Nine, Rule Six applies when the plaintiff appears but the defendant does not, at the hearing.
scenes.shown: Order IX Rule 6 applies when the plaintiff appears but the defendant does not, at the hearing.
scenes.chip: 2 · HOW A SUIT GOES EX PARTE

scenes.dialogue: If due service is proved, the court may order the suit to be heard ex parte. Otherwise, it must issue a second summons.
Before the decree, Rule Seven lets him appear at or before the adjourned hearing, show good cause, and be heard on terms.
scenes.shown: Before the decree, Rule 7 lets him appear at or before the adjourned hearing, show good cause, and be heard on terms.

scenes.dialogue: A hypothetical case. Pallavi, a paper supplier, sues Sunil, a printer, for money due on unpaid invoices.
The summons goes to a shop Sunil left two years ago. The process server reports that he affixed it to the door.
The court hears the suit ex parte and passes a money decree. Sunil first learns of it when his bank account is attached.
After the decree, Rule Thirteen lets the defendant apply to the court that passed it, for an order setting it aside.
scenes.shown: After the decree, Rule 13 lets the defendant apply to the court that passed it, for an order setting it aside.

scenes.dialogue: The court shall set the decree aside if satisfied that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing.
It may impose terms as to costs, payment into court or otherwise, and then appoints a day for proceeding with the suit.
Sunil relies on the first ground: under Order Five, Rule Seventeen, affixing is done where the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business.
scenes.shown: Sunil relies on the first ground: under Order V Rule 17, affixing is done where the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business.

scenes.dialogue: First proviso: a decree that cannot be set aside against one defendant only may be set aside against the others too.
Second proviso: a mere irregularity in service is not enough, if the defendant had notice of the hearing date and sufficient time to appear.
So if Sunil actually knew the date in time, irregular service alone will not help him.
Under the Explanation, if an appeal against the ex parte decree was disposed of other than by withdrawal, no Rule Thirteen application lies.
scenes.shown: Under the Explanation, if an appeal against the ex parte decree was disposed of other than by withdrawal, no Rule 13 application lies.

scenes.dialogue: Under Article One Twenty Three of the Limitation Act, you have thirty days from the date of the decree to apply.
scenes.shown: Under Article 123 of the Limitation Act, you have 30 days from the date of the decree to apply.

scenes.dialogue: But where the summons was not duly served, the thirty days run instead from when the applicant had knowledge of the decree.
scenes.shown: But where the summons was not duly served, the 30 days run instead from when the applicant had knowledge of the decree.

scenes.dialogue: If Sunil shows he was not duly served, his thirty days run from when he learnt of the decree.
scenes.shown: If Sunil shows he was not duly served, his 30 days run from when he learnt of the decree.

scenes.dialogue: Missed it? Section Five of the Limitation Act lets the court admit a late application, on sufficient cause for the delay.
scenes.shown: Missed it? Section 5 of the Limitation Act lets the court admit a late application, on sufficient cause for the delay.

scenes.dialogue: On this second ground, in G P Srivastava versus R K Raizada, the Supreme Court held that sufficient cause must be liberally construed, to do complete justice.
scenes.shown: On this second ground, in G.P. Srivastava versus R.K. Raizada, the Supreme Court held that sufficient cause must be liberally construed, to do complete justice.

scenes.dialogue: This applies particularly where no negligence or inaction is imputable to him. It is an elastic expression, and courts have wide discretion.
The cause must relate to the date the court proceeded ex parte. Earlier lapses, already overlooked, cannot be held against him.
If a defendant comes promptly, within time, and his absence was not mala fide or intentional, discretion is normally exercised in his favour.
Costs can make up for any hardship caused, and the case is then decided on its merits.
Section Ninety Six, sub section Two, also allows an appeal from an ex parte decree.
scenes.shown: Section 96(2) also allows an appeal from an ex parte decree.

scenes.dialogue: In Bhanu Kumar Jain versus Archana Kumar, the Supreme Court said a defendant may pursue both remedies simultaneously.
But if the appeal is dismissed, the decree merges with the appellate order, and the Rule Thirteen application is no longer maintainable.
scenes.shown: But if the appeal is dismissed, the decree merges with the appellate order, and the Rule 13 application is no longer maintainable.

scenes.dialogue: The converse is not true. If the Rule Thirteen application fails, the appeal survives, but he cannot reargue sufficient cause there.
scenes.shown: The converse is not true. If the Rule 13 application fails, the appeal survives, but he cannot reargue sufficient cause there.

scenes.dialogue: In that appeal, he may argue that the evidence on record did not justify the decree.
Under Rule Fourteen, no decree is set aside unless notice of the application is served on the opposite party.
scenes.shown: Under Rule 14, no decree is set aside unless notice of the application is served on the opposite party.

scenes.dialogue: If the Rule Thirteen application is rejected, an appeal lies under Order Forty Three, Rule One, clause D.
scenes.shown: If the Rule 13 application is rejected, an appeal lies under Order XLIII Rule 1(d).

scenes.dialogue: An appeal alone is not a stay. Order Forty One, Rule Five lets the appellate court stay execution for sufficient cause.
scenes.shown: An appeal alone is not a stay. Order XLI Rule 5 lets the appellate court stay execution for sufficient cause.

scenes.dialogue: So, act fast. Apply within thirty days of the decree, or of learning of it if the summons was not duly served.
scenes.shown: So, act fast. Apply within 30 days of the decree, or of learning of it if the summons was not duly served.

scenes.dialogue: Get certified copies of the order sheet and the process server's report, and check the address and manner of service.
Support sufficient cause with documents, offer costs, check whether an appeal was filed, and seek a stay of execution if needed.
